# Finding the next job, with AI — after 45

Research report and series plan for Collegica's *Aging well* section. Research date: 2026-09-10. Audience assumption: Canadian (Ontario-first) readers, 45–65, either unemployed or unhappy where they are, technically literate and skeptical.

Four research streams fed this: the GitHub open-source landscape (~30 repos), X/Twitter discourse (~20 fetched posts), the factual/legal landscape (~40 primary sources), and a survey of existing coverage (~35 pieces). The per-stream notes, with URLs, are in [`notes/`](/aging-well/research/).

---

## 1. The argument in five lines

1. **The risk for a 45–65 job seeker is duration and pay, not the headline rate.** Canada's long-term-unemployed share is 24% of all unemployed (Aug 2026) versus 17% pre-pandemic; roughly half of displaced Canadians aged 50–75 who found work again earned at least 25% less. AI's job is to shorten the search and defend the pay level — not to send more applications.
2. **The machine and the human want opposite things.** When an LLM screens, it prefers LLM-rewritten résumés ~97% of the time; when a recruiter reads, 80% reject generic AI prose. Use AI for structure and vocabulary at the screen; use your own voice and specifics for the human.
3. **The one signal AI cannot fake is a long, specific work history — and employers are re-weighting toward it.** After AI cover-letter tools rolled out, the letter's predictive value fell 51% and weight shifted to prior work. That is the reader's advantage, if the history is legible.
4. **Never let it apply for you.** Auto-appliers breach LinkedIn's terms (23.5M automated sessions flagged in one quarter), feed the flood recruiters are filtering against (244 applications per posting, up from 116 in 2022), and answer knockout questions with garbage. The two most-starred open-source projects both refuse to auto-submit.
5. **Nobody has written the search as a system.** AARP owns the beginner tool-tour; the second-act book canon is pre-AI; prompt packs are interchangeable. The gaps — privacy of career data, local models, a version-controlled "career repo", measuring whether AI helped, the Ontario AI-disclosure rule read from the candidate's side, the overqualified mechanism, the Mind pillar of a long search — map almost one-to-one onto habits Collegica has already published for money and health.

---

## 2. Why now — the numbers

### Canada
- **Long-term unemployment (27+ weeks):** 24.0% of ~1.5M unemployed (Aug 2026), vs. 22.5% (Apr), 22.8% (Feb) and a 2017–2019 average of 17.1%. — StatCan Labour Force Survey.
- **55+ unemployment rate:** 4.9–5.2% through 2026 — *lower* than all-ages, which is exactly why the rate misleads. June 2026 saw 55+ employment fall 47,000.
- **Re-employment pay:** among displaced Canadians 50–75 who returned to work, ~half earned ≥25% less; 15% named age as the barrier outright. — StatCan 89-646-X; IRPP.
- **Who is absorbing the rise:** workers 45+ were roughly 40% of the June-2024→June-2025 increase in Canadian unemployment. — RBC via Globe and Mail, Mar 2026.
- **Still to pull before publishing:** the age-specific long-term share, StatCan Table 14-10-0342-01.

### United States (for comparison, and because most sources are American)
- Long-term-unemployed share, July 2026: 23.4% of jobseekers 16–54 vs. **28.3% of 55+**. — AARP Employment Data Digest / BLS A-36.
- 55–64 average 26 weeks unemployed vs. 19 for 25–34; of 50–65s laid off in the past decade, 24% never found another job; 60+ perceived odds of finding a job hit a record low 43% (NY Fed, Dec 2025). — WSJ via Fortune *(snippet-grade)*.
- **Age bias in the search:** 37% of 50+ job seekers experienced it in 2025, up from 30% in 2024; 64% have seen or experienced it at work. — AARP 2025.
- **The new mechanism:** post-ChatGPT, 55+ workers in AI-exposed jobs (programmers +25%, accountants +22%) exit more — and the exits show up as *unemployment, not retirement*. Only 18% of 50–64-year-olds use generative AI. — Center for Retirement Research, Boston College, June 2026.
- **Audit-study baseline:** 40,000 fictitious applications; callbacks fall with age, worst for women and ~65; implicit cues (graduation year, dated tools, "25 years of…") lower callbacks even when age is never stated. — Neumark, Burn & Button; Frontiers 2017.

## 3. What the employer's AI actually does

**Myth:** the ATS auto-rejects résumés without the right keywords; 75% are never seen by a human.
**Reality:** ~92% of recruiters say the ATS does not auto-reject on content. The only true auto-filters are **knockout questions** (work authorization, licence, location, salary range — 84% of recruiters use them). The real silent failure is **parsing**: two-column layouts, tables, text boxes, headers/footers and image PDFs come out scrambled. A missing keyword makes you *unsearchable*, not deleted. The "75%" figure is unsourced vendor marketing.

**What is actually changing:** AI *ranking* layered on top — Workday HiredScore, LinkedIn's Hiring Assistant (recruiters review 62% fewer profiles), Indeed Talent Scout, Greenhouse AI. Ranking is where age leaks in: graduation dates, tenure length, years-of-experience fields, legacy-tool vocabulary, and LLM self-preference for LLM-written text.

**Volume:** Greenhouse, 640M applications across 6,000 companies — applications per posting rose from 116 (2022) to 244 (2025); recruiting teams shrank ~55%; 34% of recruiters spend up to half their week filtering "AI spam." 74% of job seekers use AI; 49% sent *more* applications specifically to beat filters. That is the doom loop.

### The law, in order
| When | What | Why it matters to the reader |
|---|---|---|
| Aug 2023 | **EEOC v. iTutorGroup** settles — software auto-rejected women 55+ and men 60+; first EEOC AI-hiring settlement, and it was an *age* case | Proof the mechanism exists |
| Jul 2023 | **NYC Local Law 144** — annual bias audit + notice for automated hiring tools | Still the only law that mandates an audit by name |
| May 2025 → | **Mobley v. Workday** (N.D. Cal.) — nationwide ADEA collective certified for applicants 40+ screened by Workday since Sept 2020; extended to HiredScore features (Jul 2025); the AI *vendor* can be sued directly as the employer's agent; Workday's own filings put rejections through its software at 1.1 billion. Still live (rulings Mar, May, Jun 2026) | The anchor story on X and in the press; "if you're over 40 and applied to a Fortune 500 in the last 7 years, you may be in the class" |
| 2025 | EEOC technical guidance on AI adverse impact withdrawn | Guidance ≠ law; the ADEA still applies |
| **Jan 1, 2026** | **Ontario, Working for Workers Four Act** — employers with 25+ staff must disclose in the posting if AI screens/assesses/selects applicants; must post a salary range; must say whether the vacancy is real; may not require "Canadian experience"; must tell interviewees the outcome within 45 days | **The most reader-usable lever in this report, and nobody has written it up from the candidate's side** |
| Aug 2, 2026 | **EU AI Act** — CV screening/ranking is high-risk; notice, human oversight, bias testing, logging | Applies to EU-headquartered employers and global ATS deployments |
| May 2026 | New suit alleging IBM's screening software encoded age bias | Second live age case |

Federally, Canada has no AI-specific hiring statute (AIDA died with Bill C-27 in early 2025 — verify date); age is a protected ground under the Ontario Human Rights Code and the Canadian Human Rights Act whether a human or a model decided.

---

## 4. What the evidence says works

- **Writing assistance raises hires — modestly and honestly.** ~480,000 job seekers randomized to algorithmic writing help on their profiles: +8% probability of being hired, no drop in employer satisfaction; the effect comes from *clarity*, not inflation. — van Inwegen, Munyikwa & Horton 2023.
- **AI cover letters raise callbacks, then the signal decays.** Access to an AI letter tool: +0.43 pp callbacks (+6%); for actual users ~+51%. Time spent *editing* the draft predicted success. After rollout, the correlation between letter–job alignment and callbacks fell 51% — employers stopped trusting the letter and re-weighted **prior work history**. — Cui, Dias & Ye 2025. *This is the series' core argument for a 45–65 reader.*
- **The machine prefers machine prose.** 2,245 human résumés rewritten by seven LLMs; when an LLM judges, it picks the LLM version 96–98% of the time (GPT-4o: 97.6%), even where human graders rated the original clearer; models also prefer their *own* output. — UMD/NUS/OSU study, via the most-shared X post on the topic (24k likes).
- **The human punishes it.** 800+ hiring managers: 80% reject generic AI output; 63% accept AI-*assisted* letters that are personalized; tells are "proven track record," "detail-oriented professional," "I am writing to express my interest," no numbers, no company specifics. Recruiter anecdote: eleven consecutive letters opening "I am thrilled to apply." — TopResume 2026 *(via vendor blog; primary not fetched)*; Raath; Scoble relaying Allie Miller.
- **The interview is where AI résumés die.** 65% of HR leaders find claimed skills harder to verify; 41% of employers moving away from résumé-first hiring; startups reverting to multi-day in-office work trials ("took HR 100 years to rediscover apprenticeships" — a16z's Andrew Chen). *Prove-it-live favours people who can do the job on the spot.*
- **Referrals dominate.** ~7% of applicants, 30–50% of hires; convert at ~28–34% vs. 2–5% from boards; ~10× cold applications. — SHRM; Labour Economics 2024. (Avoid the "85% of jobs are filled by networking" figure — it traces to a 2016 LinkedIn survey.)
- **Benchmarks for a personal funnel:** ~3% of applicants get an interview (CareerPlug, 10M applications); ~1 hire per 180 applicants; interview→offer 27–47% by source; 44% hear back within two weeks.
- **Usage by age:** OpenAI's own data (600k conversations) — older users *leverage* career capital (résumé refinement, recruiter outreach); younger users *build* it (interview prep, strategy). A useful frame for the whole series.

## 5. The tools

### Commercial
| Tool | Price | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| LinkedIn Premium Career | US$29.99/mo | AI job-fit summaries, profile writer; "2.6× hire likelihood" is a vendor claim. The employer-side Hiring Assistant means the first pass on LinkedIn hires is now a model. |
| Indeed Career Scout | free | Coach + résumé keywording + mock interviews; "7× faster" is self-reported |
| Teal / Huntr / Simplify | strong free tiers | Trackers + autofill (autofill ≠ auto-apply). Huntr's free tier is the most generous. |
| Jobscan | ~$50/mo | Single-purpose keyword scoring; trains keyword-stuffing |
| LazyApply / Sonara / AIHawk-style auto-appliers | $99–249+ | Breach LinkedIn §8.2; tiered restriction → permanent; "ignore screening questions or fill them with generic garbage" |

Position: a general model (hosted or local) plus a free tracker does everything the paid stack does, for a reader willing to write their own prompts — which is the Collegica reader.

### Open source (GitHub) — the state of play
Three shifts since 2024: (1) the centre of gravity moved from *bots that apply* to *AI that prepares, you submit* — the two most-starred projects, **career-ops** (71k, MIT) and **MadsLorentzen/ai-job-search** (42k, MIT), both refuse to auto-submit, and AIHawk (30k) quietly pivoted away from LinkedIn; (2) "runs inside your AI coding CLI" is the new distribution model — powerful, cheap, and a wall for a non-technical reader; (3) platforms fight back — LinkedIn flagged 23.5M automated sessions in Q1 2026; Indeed/Glassdoor speed-profile submissions.

**Top 5 worth a non-technical reader's time**
1. **Reactive Resume — rxresu.me** (42k, MIT): free, hosted, no account, privacy-first, exports PDF/DOCX/JSON. The one tool to actually use this weekend.
2. **OpenResume's ATS parser test — open-resume.com** (8.9k; stale but live): upload the PDF you've been sending, see what the machine reads. The single most eye-opening 60 seconds for anyone with a 2008-era two-column résumé.
3. **freehire.me** (653, MIT): 3.3M postings pulled straight from employer career pages / 92 ATSs (Workday, Greenhouse, Lever) — the postings that never get boosted on LinkedIn, and no automation on your own account.
4. **career-ops** (71k, MIT) — *as a method, not an install*: its A–H evaluation rubric and 1–5 fit score, its refusal to spam, its "analyze rejection patterns" step. The rubric translates directly into a paste-able prompt.
5. **Resume-Matcher** (28k, Apache-2.0) — for the one-in-ten reader (or their adult child) who'll run one Docker command: local Ollama option, keyword gap, tailored draft, interview prep, all on your own machine.

**Gaps that are Collegica's opening:** no open-source tool targets *behavioural / experienced-hire* interviewing (everything is Big-Tech coding-flavoured); only two tiny repos (ats-resume-agent, imprintcv) treat "no fabricated bullets" as a design constraint; the best evaluation method (career-ops) is trapped behind a terminal.

**Warn readers about:** README-only "open source" that sells a $9.99 extension (lookr-fyi, 467 stars); SEO-farm "Best LinkedIn Auto Apply Bot 2026" repos; archived JobFunnel; three unrelated projects named ApplyPilot; and the quiet one — most tailoring tools will happily invent a metric, and a reader with a 25-year record has the most to lose in a background check.

## 6. What X is saying

Access caveat: no authenticated X access; posts were discovered via search and fetched verbatim through public syndication mirrors (fxtwitter/vxtwitter); threads and replies were not retrievable.

- **Mobley v. Workday dominates the age conversation** — Aakash Gupta's explainer (10.5k likes), Polymarket/Reuters on the June 2026 ruling (13.5k). The most viral post of all — "our AI screener rejected 100% of pre-2010 graduates" (24k likes) — is a **legal-satire account**; it spread because it matches what people believe. Do not cite it.
- **Two audiences, opposite tastes** is live on X too: Nav Toor's post on the 97.6% LLM self-preference study (24k likes) vs. Scoble/Allie Miller ("don't use AI to write your résumé — they can tell") and Matt Stauffer's hiring round ("wild how many people just have their AI answer all the questions", 461k views).
- **Recruiter-side hedge:** demonstrable AI *fluency* — being able to talk about using AI in your work — matters more than AI-written prose (Random Recruiter: 56% wage premium for AI-skilled workers).
- **"Prove it live" is back** (work trials, probing follow-ups) as the response to AI-generated everything.
- **Commercial SaaS trackers are barely discussed on X**; prompt packs and open-source bots dominate. No first-person 50+ AI-job-search story surfaced on X — that voice lives on Substack, LinkedIn and Reddit.
- **Canadian voices are thin**: one Toronto-MBA-can't-get-an-interview post (744 likes), one 🇨🇦-flagged career coach (The Jobfather: feed the About page + ad + résumé, then *edit*). The Canadian X conversation is about youth unemployment, not 50+.

---

## 7. What's already written — and the gaps

**Covered well (don't redo):** generic prompt lists; "AI can help with résumé/cover letter/interview" tool tours (AARP, Forbes); ageism-exists trend pieces (Inc., Glassdoor +133% ageism mentions); hide-your-age résumé checklists (AARP's "age-proof" list is the most-cited in the space).

**The incumbents:** AARP owns "AI for the 50+ search" at beginner level — plain-spoken, US-only, tool-centric, silent on privacy, local models, measurement and when *not* to use AI. The second-act book canon (*The 100-Year Life*, *Second-Act Careers*, *Unretirement*) is entirely pre-AI. The best Substack pieces (Nate's evidence-first bullet; Poddar's "Career Evidence File" — "80% of the work happens before you open Claude") have the right architecture but no versioning, measurement or privacy. The Globe's "second act as a financial hedge" (Mar 2026) is the one Canadian piece that maps onto OWL's Money pillar — and mentions "free AI tools" once, unnamed.

**Ten gaps, ranked by how empty the field is**
1. **Privacy of your career history in a hosted model.** Not one consumer piece. What ChatGPT/Claude/Gemini retain by default (training on by default; ~30-day retention even opted out), how to turn it off, what to redact, when to run local. A direct transfer of the "ratios, not identifiers" rule the site already published for money.
2. **Running a local model for the sensitive steps.** An 8B model on a recent laptop is good enough for résumé work (XDA, May 2026, made the case for *quality*, not privacy). Nobody has said: evidence file and gap explanations locally; hosted model only for public-information research.
3. **The search as an engineering project — a career repo.** `evidence.md`, `master-resume.md`, `applications/<company>-<role>/` (posting, tailored résumé, note, outcome), `log.md`, a commit per change. Exactly the plans-as-documents habit the aging-well article prescribes. Written only by developers, for developers, and never for a whole search.
4. **Measuring whether AI helped.** Everyone has anecdotes ("78% got interviews" — vendor survey). Nobody proposes tagging each application with which steps used AI and watching response rate by tag, one experiment at a time, two-week stop rule. A reader with a spreadsheet can run their own n=40 trial.
5. **Reading Ontario's posting rules as a candidate.** Since Jan 2026 the posting must say whether AI screens you, the pay range, and whether the job is real. Coverage is 100% employer-compliance. A candidate playbook does not exist.
6. **The "overqualified / too senior" problem, mechanically.** Why an LLM ranker demotes a 20-year career (embedding similarity to a "5–7 years" posting; training priors — Melbourne's probe had ChatGPT put the ideal cutoff at 45) and the honest trade-off: conceal, target roles where seniority *is* the ask, or write the résumé as "the judgment you can't get from a junior plus AI."
7. **How screening bias actually works against you and what changes it.** Date proxies, keyword recency, legacy-tech tokens, LLM self-preference; what's litigated and regulated; what a candidate can do — referral channels that bypass the ranker, A/B two résumé versions, the human-review Ontario implies.
8. **The Mind pillar of a long search.** AARP's "stay focused" piece is separate from its "use AI" piece. The OWL frame joins them: 26% of unemployed 55+ are 6+ months out; a repo with a weekly review and a visible funnel is itself the routine; novel-skill learning during the search counts twice.
9. **Bridge work into semi-retirement as the actual target.** Fractional/portfolio content is executive-only (fractional execs 60k→120k, 2022–24) and AI-free. For a 58-year-old mid-level professional: package 25 years into 2–3 sellable offers, find the informal demand, price it against CPP/OAS/RRSP timing.
10. **When not to use AI at all.** Only Raath and Nate say it plainly: never let it write a claim you can't defend in a behavioural interview.

## 8. The proposed series

**Working series title:** *Finding the next job, with AI* — a companion to *Planning to Age Well, with AI*. Same house rules: method not advice; plan in ratios, not identifiers; treat plans as documents under version control; every article ends with something you can run.

**Series thesis:** after 45, the search is a targeting problem, not a volume problem. Your 25 years are the one signal the machine can't fake and the human is re-weighting toward. AI's job is to make that history legible to a parser, defensible to a person, and to shorten the search — never to apply for you.

### Article 0 — the anchor
**"Finding Your Next Job, with AI — after 45"**
The framework piece, structurally parallel to the OWL article. The numbers (duration, pay cut, exits-as-unemployment); the two-audience insight; what AI is good at (structure, vocabulary, research, rehearsal, adherence) and not (applying, inventing, deciding, the phone call); the career repo; the privacy rule; a weekly review ritual; a first week you can start. Banner: a companion to the Mind/Muscle/Money image. Ships with the repo template.

### The eight that follow, in suggested order
| # | Working title | The question it answers | AI's role | What you can run | Canadian angle | OWL tie |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| 11 | **The long search and the mind** | How do I get through six months of this? | The repo *as* routine; novel-skill learning during the search counts twice; AI fluency as both hedge and interview story; when to talk to a human instead of a model | Mind |

### The small tools (the *budget-from-statements* precedent)
Three are worth building; each is a single browser-tab, local-first page, BYO key or local model, nothing touching LinkedIn:
1. **Parse-and-gap** (article 3): résumé + posting → what a parser sees, keyword gap, tailored draft with every claim traced to the evidence file. Skeleton: resume-typst's `portfolio.yaml` as the master format, rendered by Typst compiled to WebAssembly in the tab; the imprintcv / ats-resume-agent "no fabrication" constraint.
2. **Morning digest** (article 6): employer ATS public feeds → LLM ranks against a one-page profile → a daily Markdown digest. ToS-clean by construction.
3. **Funnel** (article 9): a CSV of applications → rates by stage, source, résumé version and AI-tag.

Plus a **career-repo template** (article 0) — a git-initialized folder with `evidence.md`, `portfolio.yaml`, `applications/`, `log.md`, and a weekly-review checklist.

### Building on resume-typst
Collegica already has the master-résumé substrate: [eLearningHub/resume-typst](https://github.com/eLearningHub/resume-typst) keeps the *content* in `portfolio.yaml` (contacts, skills, jobs with bullets and tags, education), the *look* in `settings.yaml`, and renders a PDF from a ~100-line `main.typ` on typst.app — no install. Its README already assumes the workflow the series teaches: hand a model your old résumé and `portfolio.yaml`, ask it to update the YAML, paste the result back. That is the right division of labour — the model edits data, never layout — and a YAML diff is a fabrication audit.

What it needs to become the series' backbone:
- **A single-column "parser" layout.** The current template is a two-column grid (sidebar + main), which is exactly what ATS parsers scramble (§3). Same YAML, two entry files: `human.typ` (the two-column one) and `ats.typ` (single column, no tables, dates on roles) — article 3's A/B becomes one command.
- **Move the hard-coded strings into the YAML.** The summary paragraph and the LinkedIn/GitHub link labels are still literals in `main.typ`, inherited from the upstream bare-bones-cv template; the summary in particular is the thing tailored per posting.
- **A `source` field per bullet** pointing at a line in `evidence.md` — the fabrication guard, in the data, checkable by a script.
- **Render in the browser.** Typst compiles to WebAssembly (typst.ts); the parse-and-gap tool can compile `portfolio.yaml` to PDF in the tab, fully local, which retires the typst.app upload for readers who would rather not send anything anywhere.
- **Age-aware defaults** in `settings.yaml` — `history_years: 15`, `show_education_dates: false` — so the concealment trade-off in article 5 is a switch, not a rewrite.

### Editorial rules for the series
- **Method, not advice** — the same disclaimer block as the OWL article, extended: nothing here is legal or employment advice; talk to a lawyer before signing anything, and to a human before making a life decision.
- **No fabrication, ever** — every AI-drafted claim must trace to a line in the reader's own evidence file. This is the series' non-negotiable, and its differentiator.
- **Ratios, not identifiers** — employer names, compensation, health/caregiving reasons for gaps, referees: redacted or local.
- **Never auto-submit.** Say it in every article that touches applications.
- **Canadian-first** — StatCan numbers, Ontario's posting rules, EI/BJO/CTC; US figures as comparison.
- **Measure** — every technique comes with a way to tell whether it moved the funnel.

## 9. Verify before publishing
- Canadian long-term-unemployment share **by age** — pull StatCan Table 14-10-0342-01.
- Reuters 2018 Amazon-recruiting-tool link; Bill C-27/AIDA death date; CPP early-take reduction (~0.6%/month); EI training-while-on-claim rules.
- TopResume 2026 hiring-manager survey — primary source not fetched; figures are via a vendor blog.
- "78% of ChatGPT users got an interview" and "62% reject unpersonalized AI résumés (Resume Now 2025)" — vendor surveys; cite with caveat or not at all.
- The widely circulated "HBR 2024" attribution ("models trained on historical hires prefer under-40s") — could not locate the HBR original; do not cite HBR.
- LinkedIn Premium (2.6×) and Indeed Career Scout (7×) effectiveness claims are vendor self-reports.
- No primary data found on fractional/consulting outcomes for 50+ — frame as an option with an "it's a sales job first" caveat.
- Forbes, Axios, Melbourne Pursuit and CNBC pieces were paywalled/bot-walled — figures rest on search excerpts.
